claim: Aging is a major risk factor for cognitive impairment.
source: Aging is a major risk factor for cognitive impairment.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that reflects established scientific knowledge about aging and cognitive function.

claim: Aerobic exercise benefits brain function and may promote cognitive health in older adults.
source: Aerobic exercise benefits brain function and may promote cognitive health in older adults.
evidence: This statement is supported by established scientific consensus and is presented as background knowledge.

claim: Selective vulnerability of the white matter to small vessel disease exists.
source: Selective vulnerability of the white matter to small vessel disease and a link between white matter health and cognitive function suggests a potential role for responses in deep cerebral microcirculation.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: There is a link between white matter health and cognitive function.
source: Selective vulnerability of the white matter to small vessel disease and a link between white matter health and cognitive function suggests a potential role for responses in deep cerebral microcirculation.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: In sedentary aged mice, aging caused a more severe decline in cerebral microvascular perfusion in deep (infragranular) cortical layers and subcortical white matter compared with superficial (supragranular) cortical layers.
source: In the sedentary group, aging caused a more severe decline in cerebral microvascular perfusion and oxygenation in deep (infragranular) cortical layers and subcortical white matter compared with superficial (supragranular) cortical layers.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing young (3-6 months) and aged (19-21 months) sedentary mice.

claim: In sedentary aged mice, aging caused a more severe decline in cerebral microvascular oxygenation in deep (infragranular) cortical layers and subcortical white matter compared with superficial (supragranular) cortical layers.
source: In the sedentary group, aging caused a more severe decline in cerebral microvascular perfusion and oxygenation in deep (infragranular) cortical layers and subcortical white matter compared with superficial (supragranular) cortical layers.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing young and aged sedentary mice.

claim: Five months of voluntary aerobic exercise partly renormalized microvascular perfusion in aged mice in a depth-dependent manner.
source: Five months of voluntary aerobic exercise partly renormalized microvascular perfusion and oxygenation in aged mice in a depth-dependent manner, and brought these spatial distributions closer to those of young adult sedentary mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from aged exercise mice compared to aged sedentary controls.

claim: Five months of voluntary aerobic exercise partly renormalized microvascular oxygenation in aged mice in a depth-dependent manner.
source: Five months of voluntary aerobic exercise partly renormalized microvascular perfusion and oxygenation in aged mice in a depth-dependent manner, and brought these spatial distributions closer to those of young adult sedentary mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from aged exercise mice compared to aged sedentary controls.

claim: Exercise brought spatial distributions of microvascular perfusion and oxygenation closer to those of young adult sedentary mice.
source: Five months of voluntary aerobic exercise partly renormalized microvascular perfusion and oxygenation in aged mice in a depth-dependent manner, and brought these spatial distributions closer to those of young adult sedentary mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing aged exercise mice to young sedentary mice.

claim: Microcirculatory effects of exercise were accompanied by an improvement in cognitive function.
source: These microcirculatory effects were accompanied by an improvement in cognitive function.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral test data (NORT) showing improved cognitive function in exercised mice.

claim: The cerebral white matter is significantly affected by aging.
source: The cerebral white matter is significantly affected by aging (Cees De Groot et al., 2000; de Leeuw et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Subcortical white matter has greater tissue loss due to aging compared to superficial gray matter.
source: Previous work suggests that, in comparison with superficial gray matter, subcortical white matter has greater tissue loss due to aging and is more susceptible to hypoperfusion (Gunning-Dixon et al., 2009; Hase et al., 2019; Li et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Subcortical white matter is more susceptible to hypoperfusion compared to superficial gray matter.
source: Previous work suggests that, in comparison with superficial gray matter, subcortical white matter has greater tissue loss due to aging and is more susceptible to hypoperfusion (Gunning-Dixon et al., 2009; Hase et al., 2019; Li et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: White matter lesions might impair cognitive function more than gray matter lesions.
source: Indeed, white matter lesions might impair cognitive function more than gray matter lesions (Reber et al., 2021), underscoring the importance of understanding the biological mechanisms of aging-related white matter degeneration for targeted interventions.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: CSVD is a common cause of stroke.
source: CSVD is a common cause of stroke and an important contributor to age-related cognitive decline and dementia (Pantoni, 2010; Smith and Markus, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CSVD is an important contributor to age-related cognitive decline and dementia.
source: CSVD is a common cause of stroke and an important contributor to age-related cognitive decline and dementia (Pantoni, 2010; Smith and Markus, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Most CSVD-related strokes affect subcortical white and deep gray matter.
source: Most CSVD-related strokes affect subcortical white and deep gray matter.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: CSVD plays a role in accelerating the pathogenesis of Alzheimer's disease.
source: In addition, there is increased awareness of the role of CSVD in accelerating the pathogenesis of Alzheimer's disease (AD), with some studies suggesting the possibility that white matter changes are the starting point of AD (Defrancesco et al., 2014; Esiri et al., 1999; Radanovic et al., 2013; Snowdon et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Some studies suggest that white matter changes may be the starting point of Alzheimer's disease.
source: In addition, there is increased awareness of the role of CSVD in accelerating the pathogenesis of Alzheimer's disease (AD), with some studies suggesting the possibility that white matter changes are the starting point of AD (Defrancesco et al., 2014; Esiri et al., 1999; Radanovic et al., 2013; Snowdon et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Aerobic exercise is a promising strategy to improve neurocognitive function in aging.
source: Aerobic exercise is a promising strategy to improve neurocognitive function in aging and reduce the risk of age-related neurological disorders (Barnes et al., 2003; Yaffe et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Aerobic exercise can reduce the risk of age-related neurological disorders.
source: Aerobic exercise is a promising strategy to improve neurocognitive function in aging and reduce the risk of age-related neurological disorders (Barnes et al., 2003; Yaffe et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The mean capillary RBC flux in aged sedentary mice was significantly lower than that in young sedentary mice in the white matter.
source: The mean capillary RBC flux in aged sedentary mice was significantly lower than that in young sedentary mice in the white matter (Figure 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a comparing young and aged sedentary mice.

claim: No change in capillary RBC flux was observed in cortical layers II/III and IV between young and aged sedentary mice.
source: No change was observed in cortical layers II/III and IV.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from capillary RBC flux measurements.

claim: In young sedentary mice, the mean white matter RBC flux tended to be slightly higher than the gray matter RBC flux.
source: Importantly, while in young sedentary mice, the mean white matter RBC flux tended to be slightly higher than the gray matter RBC flux, the relationship appeared reversed in aged sedentary mice, where mean RBC flux in the white matter strongly tended to be lower than RBC flux in the gray matter.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing white matter and gray matter RBC flux in young mice.

claim: In aged sedentary mice, mean RBC flux in the white matter strongly tended to be lower than RBC flux in the gray matter.
source: Importantly, while in young sedentary mice, the mean white matter RBC flux tended to be slightly higher than the gray matter RBC flux, the relationship appeared reversed in aged sedentary mice, where mean RBC flux in the white matter strongly tended to be lower than RBC flux in the gray matter.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing white matter and gray matter RBC flux in aged mice.

claim: The microcirculation in the white matter is affected more than microcirculation in the gray matter by age-related changes.
source: This suggests that the microcirculation in the white matter is affected more than microcirculation in the gray matter by age-related changes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing differential effects of aging on white matter versus gray matter RBC flux.

claim: Aged exercise group showed higher capillary flux compared with sedentary controls, which was most prominent in white matter.
source: We found higher capillary flux in the aged exercise group compared with sedentary controls, which was most prominent in white matter (Figure 1a) and to a lesser extent in layer IV, while no change was observed in cortical layers II/III.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a comparing aged exercise and aged sedentary mice.

claim: Exercise increased capillary flux to a lesser extent in layer IV compared to white matter.
source: We found higher capillary flux in the aged exercise group compared with sedentary controls, which was most prominent in white matter (Figure 1a) and to a lesser extent in layer IV, while no change was observed in cortical layers II/III.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: No change in capillary flux was observed in cortical layers II/III between aged exercise and aged sedentary mice.
source: We found higher capillary flux in the aged exercise group compared with sedentary controls, which was most prominent in white matter (Figure 1a) and to a lesser extent in layer IV, while no change was observed in cortical layers II/III.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Exercise tended to increase capillary RBC speed in layer IV of the cortex and the underlying white matter.
source: Exercise also tended to increase capillary RBC speed in layer IV of the cortex and the underlying white matter, while no change was detected in layers II/III (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: No change in capillary RBC speed was detected in layers II/III between aged exercise and aged sedentary mice.
source: Exercise also tended to increase capillary RBC speed in layer IV of the cortex and the underlying white matter, while no change was detected in layers II/III (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: No significant difference in the RBC line-density between aged sedentary and aged exercise groups was found.
source: No significant difference in the RBC line-density between aged sedentary and aged exercise groups was found (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The RBC line-density of subcortical white matter was significantly higher than the RBC line-density of gray matter in both aged sedentary and aged exercise groups.
source: The RBC line-density of subcortical white matter was significantly higher than the RBC line-density of gray matter in both aged sedentary and aged exercise groups, consistent with the previous numerical simulation result (Gould et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and is consistent with a cited simulation study.

claim: Exercise decreased the coefficient of variation (CV) of capillary RBC flux in subcortical white matter but not the gray matter.
source: Exercise decreased the coefficient of variation (CV) of capillary RBC flux in subcortical white matter but not the gray matter, suggesting more homogeneous microvascular blood flow in white matter in the aged exercise group (Figure 1c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Exercise suggests more homogeneous microvascular blood flow in white matter in the aged exercise group.
source: Exercise decreased the coefficient of variation (CV) of capillary RBC flux in subcortical white matter but not the gray matter, suggesting more homogeneous microvascular blood flow in white matter in the aged exercise group (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the decreased CV of capillary RBC flux in white matter.

claim: A strong correlation was found between the venular flow and the vessel diameter in both aged sedentary and aged exercise groups.
source: As expected, a strong correlation was found between the venular flow and the vessel diameter in both groups, consistent with the previous observation of positive correlation between venular flow speed and the vessel diameter in mice (Santisakultarm et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and is consistent with a cited previous study.

claim: The regression slope for the aged exercise group was steeper than that for the sedentary group (p = 0.005).
source: Importantly, the regression slope for the aged exercise group was steeper than that for the sedentary group (p = 0.005, analysis of covariance).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Blood flow in ascending venules was significantly larger (by ~46%) in the aged exercise group compared to sedentary controls.
source: Blood flow in ascending venules was significantly larger (by ~46%) in the aged exercise group compared to sedentary controls (Figure 1e).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: The capillary RBC flux in subcortical white matter was moderately negatively correlated with the average daily running distance (R2 = 0.31).
source: The capillary RBC flux in subcortical white matter was moderately negatively correlated with the average daily running distance (i.e., exercise intensity; R2 = 0.31).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of experimental data.

claim: No strong correlation was found between other measured parameters and the exercise intensity.
source: No strong correlation was found between other measured parameters and the exercise intensity (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Resting-state capillary mean pO2 gradually increased from layer I to IV by ~6 mmHg in young adult mice (3–5 months old).
source: We have previously shown that the resting-state capillary mean pO2 gradually increased from layer I to IV by ~6 mmHg in young adult mice (3–5 months old) of the same strain and sex (Li et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Aged sedentary mice exhibited a different pattern of capillary mean pO2, with the capillary mean pO2 reaching a plateau in layers II/III.
source: In contrast, the aged sedentary mice here exhibited a different pattern, with the capillary mean pO2 reaching a plateau in layers II/III (capillary mean pO2, layer I: 42 ± 1 mmHg, layers II/III: 46 ± 1 mmHg, layer IV: 45 ± 2 mmHg).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from aged sedentary mice.

claim: The aged exercise group showed an overall increase in capillary mean pO2 in comparison with the aged sedentary group across all cortical layers.
source: The aged exercise group showed an overall increase in capillary mean pO2 in comparison with the aged sedentary group across all cortical layers (Figure 2a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The pO2 increase in cortical layer IV was more pronounced compared to the other layers in aged exercise mice.
source: The pO2 increase in cortical layer IV was more pronounced compared to the other layers.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing pO2 changes across cortical layers.

claim: The distribution of capillary pO2 in the aged exercise group shifted toward higher pO2 compared with aged sedentary controls.
source: The distribution of capillary pO2 in the aged exercise group also shifted toward higher pO2 compared with aged sedentary controls (Figure 2b and Figure 2—figure supplement 1), which was again more pronounced in layer IV.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: A strong positive correlation was found between the mean pO2 and mean capillary RBC flux in both aged sedentary and aged exercise groups.
source: Consistent with our previous report (Li et al., 2019), we also found a strong positive correlation between the mean pO2 and mean capillary RBC flux in both groups (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and is consistent with a cited previous study.

claim: A moderate but statistically insignificant increase in Hct was observed in the aged exercise group compared with aged sedentary mice.
source: We observed a moderate but statistically insignificant increase in Hct in the aged exercise group compared with aged sedentary mice (Figure 2c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The pO2 and SO2 in the diving cortical arterioles and ascending venules across cortical layers were lower in the aged sedentary mice than in young adult mice.
source: The pO2 and the oxygen saturation of hemoglobin (SO2) in the diving cortical arterioles and ascending venules across cortical layers were lower in the aged sedentary mice (Figure 2d–g) than what we have reported in young adult mice (Li et al., 2019), and in agreement with the pO2 values in old mice previously reported by others (Moeini et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d-g and is consistent with cited previous studies.

claim: Both pO2 and SO2 tended to increase in all cortical layers in aged exercise group compared with aged sedentary group, particularly in layer IV.
source: Importantly, both pO2 and SO2 tended to increase in all cortical layers in aged exercise group compared with aged sedentary group, particularly in layer IV, consistent with the largest changes in the capillary RBC flux and mean pO2 observed in the deeper cortical layers.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and is consistent with other measurements in the study.

claim: The depth-dependent oxygen extraction fraction (DOEF) decreased in the aged exercise group compared with the aged sedentary controls, with potentially the largest decrease in the layer IV.
source: Consequently, the depth-dependent oxygen extraction fraction (DOEF) decreased in the aged exercise group compared with the aged sedentary controls, with potentially the largest decrease in the layer IV (Figure 2h).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2h.

claim: The peak amplitudes of the hemodynamic response were significantly smaller in aged mice compared with young sedentary mice regardless of the exercise status.
source: The peak amplitudes of the hemodynamic response were significantly smaller in aged mice compared with young sedentary mice regardless of the exercise status (Figure 3c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Exercise did not affect the peak response amplitude of the hemodynamic response.
source: However, the exercise did not affect the peak response amplitude.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing aged sedentary and aged exercise groups.

claim: Response latency (time to peak after stimulus onset) did not differ among the aged sedentary, aged exercise, and young sedentary groups.
source: Response latency (i.e., time to peak after stimulus onset) also did not differ among the groups (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both young sedentary and aged exercise mice had significantly higher microvascular segment density in the cortical layers I–IV, compared with aged sedentary mice.
source: Both young sedentary and aged exercise mice had significantly higher microvascular segment and length density in the cortical layers I–IV, compared with their aged sedentary mice (Figure 4b, c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Both young sedentary and aged exercise mice had significantly higher microvascular length density in the cortical layers I–IV, compared with aged sedentary mice.
source: Both young sedentary and aged exercise mice had significantly higher microvascular segment and length density in the cortical layers I–IV, compared with their aged sedentary mice (Figure 4b, c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Mice from the aged exercise group spent more time exploring the novel object than the familiar one leading to significantly higher discrimination index (DI) scores across four different time intervals than aged sedentary mice.
source: In the novel object recognition test (NORT), mice from the aged exercise group spent more time exploring the novel object than the familiar one leading to significantly higher discrimination index (DI) scores across four different time intervals than aged sedentary mice (Figure 5a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from NORT shown in Figure 5a.

claim: The DI score for each time interval correlated with the average daily running distance.
source: Interestingly, the DI score for each time interval correlated with the average daily running distance (Figure 5b–e).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5b-e.

claim: Aged sedentary and aged exercise groups did not differ in the Y-maze test performance.
source: In contrast, aged sedentary and aged exercise groups did not differ in the Y-maze test performance (Figure 5f).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Y-maze test shown in Figure 5f.

claim: In aged sedentary mice, the capillary RBC flux in the subcortical white matter tended to be lower than that in the gray matter.
source: In aged sedentary mice, the capillary RBC flux in the subcortical white matter tended to be lower than that in the gray matter (Figure 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Young sedentary mice showed the opposite trend, with higher capillary RBC flux in the subcortical white matter compared to the gray matter.
source: Young sedentary mice showed the opposite trend, consistent with our previous finding in anesthetized young adult mice (3–5 months old) showing a higher capillary RBC flux in the subcortical white matter compared to the gray matter (Li et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and is consistent with a cited previous study.

claim: A large discrepancy in the capillary RBC flux between young and aged sedentary mice was observed in the white matter with preserved capillary RBC flux in the superficial gray matter.
source: Importantly, we observed a large discrepancy in the capillary RBC flux between young and aged sedentary mice in the white matter with preserved capillary RBC flux in the superficial gray matter.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing young and aged sedentary mice.

claim: Cerebral white matter is more susceptible to hypoperfusion compared to the gray matter, potentially because it is located further downstream with respect to the arterial blood supply.
source: Cerebral white matter is known to be more susceptible to hypoperfusion compared to the gray matter, potentially because it is located further downstream with respect to the arterial blood supply (Gunning-Dixon et al., 2009; Markus et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies and includes a mechanistic explanation.

claim: White matter vulnerability to ischemic injury increases with age.
source: White matter vulnerability to ischemic injury increases with age (Baltan et al., 2008), and white matter lesions and lacunar infarcts are common in elderly people with CSVD and hypertension (Breteler et al., 1994; van Swieten et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: White matter lesions and lacunar infarcts are common in elderly people with CSVD and hypertension.
source: White matter vulnerability to ischemic injury increases with age (Baltan et al., 2008), and white matter lesions and lacunar infarcts are common in elderly people with CSVD and hypertension (Breteler et al., 1994; van Swieten et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Five months of exercise restored the spatial distribution trend of capillary RBC flux close to its distribution in the young sedentary mice.
source: Five months of exercise restored the spatial distribution trend of capillary RBC flux close to its distribution in the young sedentary mice (Figure 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Exercise was associated with a decreased CV of the capillary RBC flux in subcortical white matter, suggesting more homogeneous microvascular blood flow in that region.
source: Exercise was associated with a decreased CV of the capillary RBC flux in subcortical white matter, suggesting more homogeneous microvascular blood flow in that region that could potentially facilitate improved oxygen delivery to tissue.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and includes an inference about oxygen delivery.

claim: Increased capillary perfusion in the white matter was accompanied by increased blood flow in ascending venules.
source: Increased capillary perfusion in the white matter was accompanied by increased blood flow in ascending venules, as measured by Doppler OCT (Figure 1d, e).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1d and 1e.

claim: Large venules likely extend further to subcortical white matter where the increased capillary perfusion was observed.
source: In contrast to smaller ascending venules having their branches being distributed mostly over the upper cortical layers, large venules likely extend further to subcortical white matter where the increased capillary perfusion was observed (Duvernoy et al., 1981; Kirst et al., 2020; Xiong et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies describing vascular anatomy.

claim: Previous studies in mice reported conflicting results regarding the effects of exercise on cortical microcirculation.
source: Previous studies in mice reported conflicting results regarding the effects of exercise on cortical microcirculation (Dorr et al., 2017; Falkenhain et al., 2020; Lu et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Previous observations on exercise effects have been limited to the blood flow in gray matter.
source: However, these observations have been limited to the blood flow in gray matter, which was shown in this study to be less responsive to exercise than that in deeper brain regions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the current study's findings and previous literature.

claim: Human MRI data acquired after short-term (1 week) exercise showed that exercise induced a selective increase in hippocampal CBF with no or negligible changes in the gray matter CBF.
source: Human MRI data acquired after short-term (1 week) exercise showed that exercise induced a selective increase in hippocampal CBF with no or negligible changes in the gray matter CBF (Steventon et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Cerebral subcortical microcirculation is more responsive to both age-related and exercise-induced changes than cortical microcirculation.
source: Our findings suggest that cerebral subcortical microcirculation is more responsive to both age-related and exercise-induced changes than cortical microcirculation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in the study.

claim: In aged sedentary mice, the mean capillary pO2 increased from layer I to II/III and reached a plateau in layer II/III.
source: In aged sedentary mice, the mean capillary pO2 increased from layer I to II/III and reached a plateau in layer II/III (Figure 2a, b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a and 2b.

claim: Young sedentary mice showed a gradual increase in the mean capillary pO2 from layer I to IV.
source: A different trend was observed in young sedentary mice, which showed a gradual increase in the mean capillary pO2 from layer I to IV (Li et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Mice from the aged exercise group showed a similar trend to young sedentary mice, with a pronounced increase in the mean capillary pO2 in layer IV among all assessed cortical layers.
source: In contrast to aged sedentary controls, mice from the aged exercise group showed a similar trend to young sedentary mice, with a pronounced increase in the mean capillary pO2 in layer IV among all assessed cortical layers.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing aged exercise mice to young sedentary mice.

claim: In the mouse somatosensory cortex, layer IV exhibits the highest neuronal and capillary densities and the strongest staining for the cytochrome c oxidase.
source: In the mouse somatosensory cortex, layer IV exhibits the highest neuronal and capillary densities and the strongest staining for the cytochrome c oxidase, potentially implying the highest oxidative demand during activation and/or at rest throughout all cortical layers (Blinder et al., 2013; Lefort et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: High plaque load and decreased blood vessel density were observed, particularly in layer IV of the somatosensory cortex in aged, 18-month-old transgenic AD mice.
source: In an immunohistochemical study performed using an anti-Glut-1 antibody, high plaque load and decreased blood vessel density were observed, particularly in layer IV of the somatosensory cortex in aged, 18-month-old transgenic AD mice, while younger AD mice did not demonstrate any difference compared to the wild-type mice (Kuznetsova and Schliebs, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The decrease in capillary mean pO2 in layer IV in aged sedentary mice could be associated with the larger mismatch in the oxygen delivery and consumption compared with the more superficial cortical layers.
source: The decrease in capillary mean pO2 in layer IV in aged sedentary mice could be associated with the larger mismatch in the oxygen delivery and consumption compared with the more superficial cortical layers.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the experimental data and known characteristics of layer IV.

claim: Voluntary exercise significantly improved microvascular oxygenation compared to sedentary controls, particularly in layer IV.
source: Voluntary exercise significantly improved microvascular oxygenation compared to sedentary controls, particularly in layer IV.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing aged exercise and aged sedentary mice.

claim: Exercise differentially affected cortical intravascular oxygenation, with the largest increase in the deeper layers.
source: Similar to our finding of capillary RBC flux improvement due to exercise mostly in the white matter, exercise differentially affected cortical intravascular oxygenation, with the largest increase in the deeper layers and restored the spatial distribution trend of capillary pO2 across cortical layers close to its distribution in the young sedentary mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing depth-dependent effects of exercise.

claim: The RBC line-density in both groups of aged mice was significantly higher in the subcortical white matter than in the gray matter.
source: Interestingly, we found that the RBC line-density in both groups of aged mice was significantly higher in the subcortical white matter than in the gray matter.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from aged mice.

claim: Higher RBC line-density in subcortical white matter was not observed in young adult mice.
source: This was not observed in young adult mice (Li et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: The finding of higher RBC line-density in white matter is consistent with previous simulation results that showed higher Hct levels in deep-reaching penetrating arterioles compared to arterioles whose branches connect to the capillary bed closer to the surface due to the plasma skimming effect.
source: However, this finding is consistent with previous simulation results that showed higher Hct levels in deep-reaching penetrating arterioles compared to arterioles whose branches connect to the capillary bed closer to the surface due to the plasma skimming effect (Gould et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous simulation study.

claim: No change in the relative peak amplitude or the latency of stimulus-induced hemodynamic response was observed with exercise.
source: Consistent with the small effect of exercise on cerebral microcirculation and oxygenation in superficial cortical areas, we observed no change in the relative peak amplitude or the latency of stimulus-induced hemodynamic response with exercise, assessed with OISI at 570 nm, which emphasizes the intrinsic signal originating from cerebral blood volume changes in the superficial cortical layers (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Malonek et al., 1997; Tian et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Young sedentary mice (7 months old) showed a significantly larger relative response amplitude than aged mice.
source: Young sedentary mice (7 months old) showed a significantly larger relative response amplitude than aged mice, consistent with the reduced cerebrovascular reactivity with age in healthy adults and rodents (Bálint et al., 2019; Barnes, 2015; Cai et al., 2023; Jessen et al., 2017; Seker et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and is consistent with cited previous studies.

claim: The aged exercise group had larger capillary density in the gray matter.
source: While no statistically significant difference in the mean capillary RBC flux in the gray matter was found between the aged sedentary and aged exercise groups (Figure 1a), the aged exercise group had larger capillary density in the gray matter (Figure 4b), suggesting that cortical blood perfusion was possibly also higher in the aged exercise group.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Cortical blood perfusion was possibly higher in the aged exercise group.
source: While no statistically significant difference in the mean capillary RBC flux in the gray matter was found between the aged sedentary and aged exercise groups (Figure 1a), the aged exercise group had larger capillary density in the gray matter (Figure 4b), suggesting that cortical blood perfusion was possibly also higher in the aged exercise group.
evidence: This is an inference based on the larger capillary density observed in the aged exercise group.

claim: Aging-associated decrease in cerebral microvascular density has been observed across brain regions in both humans and rodents.
source: Consistent with our findings, aging-associated decrease and exercise-induced increase in cerebral microvascular density have been observed across brain regions in both humans and rodents (Ding et al., 2006; Morland et al., 2017; Riddle et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Exercise-induced increase in cerebral microvascular density has been observed across brain regions in both humans and rodents.
source: Consistent with our findings, aging-associated decrease and exercise-induced increase in cerebral microvascular density have been observed across brain regions in both humans and rodents (Ding et al., 2006; Morland et al., 2017; Riddle et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Other studies showed no improvements in cerebral microvascular structure with regular exercise in the mouse sensorimotor cortex.
source: However, other studies showed no improvements in cerebral microvascular structure with regular exercise in the mouse sensorimotor cortex (Cudmore et al., 2017; Dorr et al., 2017; Falkenhain et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Significant morphological changes in the microvascular morphometric parameters were found due to chronic exercise in the somatosensory cortex of 20-month-old mice.
